name: Proto-Austronesian
notes: Inventory follows the ACD orthography (Blust et al. 2023) used in the source, ch. 3 (p. 49); phonetic values are Shibata's reconstruction (Table 6.13, p. 150). Blust's c, D, ñ and r are left out: the source finds them not well supported by Formosan languages and found in very few PAn reconstructions (pp. 5, 49). It argues against D, c and ñ on pp. 30-33; r gets no argument of its own (p. 49 n. 3 refers to Liao 2024). Blust (2013: 553-591), the Blust system: Table 8.18 (p. 554) has 25 consonants and four vowels; the diphthongs *-ay, *-aw, *-uy, *-iw are listed as sequences, not phonemes. Canonical shape CVCVC or CVCCVC, with clusters only in reduplicated monosyllables and no medial prenasalisation (p. 554). Blust rejects contrastive stress (pp. 554-563), *T (p. 567), *ʔ (pp. 567-574), *b1/*b2 (pp. 574-575), *d1-*d3 (p. 577), *Z (pp. 577-578) and subscripted *R (pp. 588-589), and leaves the evidence for *-ey and *-ew unexplained (pp. 590-591).

notes: Parent is PMP: the source rejects the interstages PEMP and PCEMP (pp. 40-46). It also argues that early POc kept a third, prenasalised obstruent series (ᵐb, ⁿd, ᵑg; also ⁿr, ñj) from PMP nasal + obstruent clusters, merged with the voiced series in POc as conventionally reconstructed (pp. 33-39), and reports a proposal by Lynch (2022) to revise the vowels (pp. 39-40). Neither revision is in the inventory entered here.

PMc is the ancestor of Kosraean, Kiribati, Marshallese and the Pohnpeic and Chuukic languages (Figure 1 (p. 3, adapted from Jackson 1983: fig. 6)); Blumenfeld (2022b: 687), following Hughes (2020a, b), adds Nauruan. name: Kosraean
orthography_note: Consonants and glides in IPA, from the phonetic notation of Lee (1975: 4-6, 18-28): orthographic sr is ʂ, r is ɻ (an approximant after Lee & Wang 1984: 436, n. 4; Lee describes a flap), y is j; velarised consonants (Lee's prime, spelled with a following w) are written with ˠ, and rounded ones (Lee's double prime, spelled with o before e and ac) with ʷ; Lee's velarised w' is written w. Bender et al. (2003a) keep Lee's orthographic sr and r; their rows are converted. Vowels: the rewriting by Bender et al. (2003a: 3, Table 1) of the digraph vowels of Lee (1976): ih → ɨ, uc → ə, ac → ε, uh → ʌ, oh → ɔ, ah → æ, oa → ɒ. This matches Lee's own phonetic values (1975: 4, 16), except that the inventory writes the IPA letter ɛ and that Lee describes oa as a low back vowel whose first part is round and last part is not (p. 15).
notes: Reflexes of the PMc consonants from Tables 2-3 of Bender et al. (2003a: 4-5), which state every row against PMc; parent_id is therefore PMc and the position in the tree is kept in subgroup_path. A primary branch of PMc in Figure 1 (p. 3, adapted from Jackson 1983: fig. 6). Data source: Lee (1976). Ross et al. (2023: 625, Appendix B.7): Kosraean, glottocode kosr1238, ISO kos, 5.31 162.98. Inventory from Lee (1975: 16, 18-28): consonants in plain, velarised and rounded series (Table 1, p. 18), five glides (p. 26) and twelve vowels, all but the low vowels occurring short or long (p. 16). Lee & Wang (1984) state about 100 cognates against POC in the orthography of Grace (1969); their consonant and vowel reflexes are entered against PMc by composing them with the POc > PMc rows of Bender et al. (2003a: 4-5) and, for the vowels, PMc's five vowels taken as POc's unchanged; each row's notes give the POC statement as printed. The velarised and rounded consonants are entered as reflexes of the same PMc consonants as the plain ones, before e and ɛ, where Lee & Wang (1984: 403-404, 415-416) find them distinctive. Not entered from Lee & Wang: POC *q (written *ʔ) > ∅ (p. 407) and *R > ∅ (p. 412), since the database has no PMc reflex of POc *q and POc *R was lost in PMc under unclear conditions; the loss of POC final consonants (p. 413), which PMc had already lost; and the many reflexes of *a that the source does not condition (pp. 421-425). In a postscript Wang suspects direct and indirect inheritance in Kosraean, as in Rotuman (p. 434).

name: Nauruan
orthography_note: No standardized orthography: several near-standards are in use (Kayser's grammar, the Nauruan Bible, the 1930s Nauruan language commission, the dictionary draft of Jacob et al. 1996, an informal online system), which differ e.g. in the velar nasal (ṅ, ñ, ng) and above all in the vowels (Blumenfeld 2022a: 653). Blumenfeld (2022a) gives forms in the Jacob et al. spelling beside a transcription: p = pʷ, p; b = bʷ, b; t; d; k; g = ɡ; q = kʷ; m = mʷ, m; n; ñ = ŋ; j; w = w, u̯; r = r, ř; ts (sometimes ds) for the affricate allophones of t, d; i = i, ɨ, i̯, j; e = e, ʌ; a = ɑ, æ; ã = e, i̯e; o = o, ʌ, u̯; õ = ʌ, ɑ, o, u̯; u and ũ = u, ɨ. The two labial series are told apart only by the spelling of the following vowel, the two rhotics not at all (pp. 673, 675-676). The forms behind the correspondences are surface forms in transcription; stress, the allophonic change t, d > ts, dz before i, and gemination of sonorants are not shown (Blumenfeld 2022b: 689).
notes: Treated as a Micronesian language descending from PMc, following Hughes (2020a, b); Jackson (1986) had excluded it from nuclear Micronesian (Blumenfeld 2022b: 687). It shares the merger of *s and *S with all Micronesian languages except Kosraean, but the source calls conclusions about subgrouping premature (pp. 687, 717). Fewer than 200 items are given etymologies and many changes are not fully regular (p. 686). A large layer of Kiribati loans (2022b section 3, pp. 713-717) is entered as loan-stratum rows: voiced ɡ, d for KIR k, t, n for *l in all environments, and ř for KIR r from *s, *S (and from *c, where the inherited reflex is ř as well). Loans usually take the noun prefix dʌ-, do- instead of e- and tend to keep final vowels; old loans have lost them and share other Nauruan changes (pp. 713-714). The inventory follows Blumenfeld (2022a): six long vowels i e æ u o ɑ and two short central vowels ɨ ʌ, which do not attract stress and surface as [u, o] before w and as [i, e] between front consonants (pp. 659, 665, 669-670); the semivowels i̯, u̯ are non-syllabic counterparts of i, u (p. 661; 2022b: 684); m, mʷ, n, r, ř have a singleton-geminate contrast (pp. 653, 657). Hughes (2020b) analyses the affricates before i as phonemes and ʌ, ɑ as allophones (2022a: 672-675). Ross et al. (2023: 626, Appendix B.7): Nauruan, glottocode naur1243, ISO nau, -0.53 166.94.

name: Proto-Coastal Formosan
orthography_note: PAn (ACD) symbols: the source writes its few reconstructions at this level (EF-MP puki, SadiRi, p. 23) in PAn orthography and gives no inventory.
notes: Working hypothesis of Chen et al. (2022): the common ancestor of East Formosan and Malayo-Polynesian, one of nine primary branches of Austronesian (Figures 2, 9 and 11; pp. 4, 20, 22). The evidence is morphosyntactic (transitive use of ma-) and lexical; the only sound change assigned to it is the merger of PAn C and t (Figure 9). The other rows are retentions implied by Figure 9, entered so that the daughters can be stated against this node. In this database PMP still has PAn as its parent.
inherit_note: Unchanged: Figure 9 (p. 20) of Chen et al. (2022) assigns this node no change to this phoneme.

(2022: 12, 20), who make it a sister of Malayo-Polynesian under Proto-Coastal Formosan (Figure 9). The source reconstructs nothing else for it and notes that Sagart (2004, 2014) disputes the subgroup (p. 13).

name: Siraya
notes: Not spoken since the early twentieth century (Adelaar 2011: 2, cited in Shibata 2025: 98); left out of the source's main discussion because the surviving transcriptions are inconsistent and the cognates few (pp. 98-99). Two dialects are cited, that of the Gospel translations and that of the Utrecht Manuscripts (Adelaar 1999, 2014; pp. 17, 103-104, 107 n. 15). Adelaar (2014) reconstructs Proto-Siraya ð and d for the PAn voiced coronal obstruents (p. 98); Proto-Siraya is not entered as a lect because the source gives no reflexes for it. Blust (1999a) puts Siraya with Kavalan, Amis and Basay in East Formosan on the merger of j and n; the source does not adopt the subgroup (pp. 7, 163).

name: Basay
notes: Extinct; the source asks for caution with its limited data (p. 142). Called a close relative of Kavalan; Tseng (2022) reconstructs their ancestor as Proto-Northern East Formosan, and Blust (1999a) puts both in East Formosan with Amis and Siraya (p. 163). The source does not adopt either subgroup (p. 7), and Kavalan is entered directly under PAn, so Basay is too.

name: Taokas
notes: One of the extinct languages of the western plains, which the source leaves out of its main discussion: they were almost extinct when recorded, show attrition and Southern Min influence (Tsuchida 2002), and the data, nearly all in Tsuchida (1982), are inconsistent (p. 99). The source treats Taokas as a language; Glottolog lists it as a dialect of Babuza. The source makes no subgrouping assumptions (p. 7), so the path stops at PAN.

name: Babuza
notes: One of the extinct languages of the western plains, which the source leaves out of its main discussion: they were almost extinct when recorded, show attrition and Southern Min influence (Tsuchida 2002), and the data, nearly all in Tsuchida (1982), are inconsistent (p. 99). Favorlang, recorded by Dutch missionaries in the 17th century, is taken by the source to be an earlier form of the same language, following Ogawa (1930a) (p. 99 n. 5); it has more data but inconsistent transcriptions. Each row says whether the source's label is Babuza or Favorlang. The source makes no subgrouping assumptions (p. 7), so the path stops at PAN.

name: Papora
notes: One of the extinct languages of the western plains, which the source leaves out of its main discussion: they were almost extinct when recorded, show attrition and Southern Min influence (Tsuchida 2002), and the data, nearly all in Tsuchida (1982), are inconsistent (p. 99). Glottolog lists Papora as a dialect of Papora-Hoanya. The source makes no subgrouping assumptions (p. 7), so the path stops at PAN.

name: Hoanya
notes: One of the extinct languages of the western plains, which the source leaves out of its main discussion: they were almost extinct when recorded, show attrition and Southern Min influence (Tsuchida 2002), and the data, nearly all in Tsuchida (1982), are inconsistent (p. 99). Hoanya is the usual collective name for Arikun and Lo’a (p. 99). Glottolog lists Hoanya as a dialect of Papora-Hoanya. The source makes no subgrouping assumptions (p. 7), so the path stops at PAN.

name: Ketagalan
notes: Named only in a passage translated from Ogawa (1931: 35-36), in quotation marks (p. 14); the source says nothing more about the language or about what Ogawa's label covers. Ketangalan is Glottolog's name. The source makes no subgrouping assumptions (p. 7), so the path stops at PAN.

name: Kaxabu
region: Western plains of Taiwan; Puli basin
notes: The second dialect of Pazeh, less conservative than Auran Pazeh (the lect entered as Pazeh), after Li & Tsuchida (2001: 2) (section 3.6, p. 67). The source states one difference only; everything else is under Pazeh. Region as given for Pazeh as a whole.

name: Proto-Celebic
orthography_note: j continues PMP z by an orthographic convention of the source (PMP *z = PCEL *j, p. 311); y continues PMP j and y; ə is PMP e (schwa); e and o are the vowels from PMP -ay and -aw.
notes: Tentative reconstruction by the source, based on Mead's (2003) six innovations (pp. 300, 311; fn. 6); reflexes from the PCEL column of Table 18 (p. 312) and sections 2 and 4.1. Not entered as rows: medial clusters C1C2 > C2 where C1 was not a nasal (Mead's innovation 1, p. 300); nasal clusters mp, mb, nt, nd, ns, ŋk are kept (Table 18). PCEL kept (almost) the full range of PMP final consonants (p. 314). The source's Celebic is Tominic, Kaili–Wolio and Eastern Celebic (Saluan–Banggai, Bungku–Tolaki, Muna–Buton), without Badaic and Rampi (pp. 299, 301). No inventory is given; this one is generated from the reflexes.

name: Proto-Kaili–Wolio
region: Central Sulawesi; homeland placed around Lake Poso (p. 320)
orthography_note: Symbols are the source's: j is the affricate [ʤ] and y the palatal glide (p. 311); ñ, ŋ and ʔ as in Table 18 (cited forms in the source spell ŋ as ng and ñ as ny). å is a vowel found only word-finally, from *a/*ə + *R.
notes: Reconstructed by the source. Vowel inventory stated in section 4.1 (p. 303); the consonants are those of the PKW column of Table 18 (p. 312), which is a table of non-final reflexes and not an inventory, plus d and g from the reconstructions. The only final consonant reconstructed is ʔ; the source leaves open whether PKW kept more final stops or final nasals (pp. 314-315). Daughters allow only NC clusters medially (p. 314).

name: Proto-Northern Kaili–Wolio
region: Central Sulawesi; homeland placed between Tentena and Poso (p. 320)
orthography_note: Symbols are the source's: j is the affricate [ʤ] and y the palatal glide (p. 311); ñ, ŋ and ʔ as in Table 18 (cited forms in the source spell ŋ as ng and ñ as ny).
notes: Northern branch: Greater Kaili (Common Kaili, Sedoa, Kulawi, Lindu), Topoiyo, Uma, Pamona (p. 302). The source gives PNKW forms throughout the appendix but no inventory; it is generated from the reflexes. Most of Martens's (1997) Proto-Kaili–Pamona reconstructions can be taken as PNKW (p. 303); the appendix cites them next to the PNKW forms. No glottocode: Glottolog's Northern Kaili-Wolio includes Ledo, which the source puts in the Southern branch.

name: Proto-Southern Kaili–Wolio
region: Sulawesi; dispersal placed in the Wotu area (p. 320)
orthography_note: Symbols are the source's: j is the affricate [ʤ] and y the palatal glide (p. 311); ñ, ŋ and ʔ as in Table 18 (cited forms in the source spell ŋ as ng and ñ as ny).
notes: Southern branch: Ledo (dominant lexical stratum), Wotu, and Island Kaili–Wolio (Wolio, Kamaru, Kalao, Loa') (p. 302). PSKW forms are given in the appendix but no inventory; it is generated from the reflexes. Not entered as rows: an added w in two etyma, PKW *uaʔ > PSKW *uwa 'vein' and *ue > *uwe 'water' (Table 23, p. 316). No glottocode: Glottolog's Southern Kaili-Wolio does not include Ledo.

name: Wolio
subgroup_path: Austronesian > Malayo-Polynesian > Celebic > Kaili–Wolio > Southern Kaili–Wolio > Island Kaili–Wolio
orthography_note: The source writes the implosive /ɓ/ as b throughout (fn. 26); entered here as ɓ.
notes: Wolio has converged with the Muna–Buton languages and has many loans from them (pp. 315, 318); final -o for PMP *ə marks such loans (fn. 2, fn. 10). Single loans named by the source and not entered as rows: seli 'dig' from Muna (p. 318), raha 'branch' and hole 'roast' from Cia-Cia or Muna (pp. 343), tepi 'winnow' from Muna (p. 343).

name: Loa'
subgroup_path: Austronesian > Malayo-Polynesian > Celebic > Kaili–Wolio > Southern Kaili–Wolio > Island Kaili–Wolio
notes: Loa' (Barang-Barang) is a language for the source (pp. 301-302); Glottolog has Barang-Barang as a dialect of Laiyolo. Strong Selayarese influence: loans have final ʔ and ŋ, geminates and ʔC clusters, while the inherited stratum is fully vocalic (pp. 314, 318). The cited forms have ə in non-final syllables (pənosa, kəpeo, bəlua); the source does not state a rule.

name: Wotu
notes: Strongly influenced by Bugis; geminate consonants occur in loans, the inherited stratum is fully vocalic (pp. 314-315).

name: Ledo
notes: A mixed lect for the source (pp. 302, 316-317): a Common Kaili (Northern) lect in morphology and syntax with a predominantly Southern lexical stratum. The source lists it under Southern Kaili–Wolio 'dominant lexical stratum', so reflexes are entered against PSKW; the Northern-stratum outcomes of Tables 25-26 are entered as loan-stratum rows against the PSKW phoneme of the same etymon. Glottolog classifies Ledo Kaili under Northern Kaili-Wolio (Common Kaili).

name: Da'a
subgroup_path: Austronesian > Malayo-Polynesian > Celebic > Kaili–Wolio > Northern Kaili–Wolio > Greater Kaili > Common Kaili
notes: Represents Common Kaili (all Kaili lects other than Ledo, p. 302) in Table 18. The prose statements about Common Kaili (voicing of stops after nasals, retention of j, p. 311) agree with the Da'a column. The source also says s > h in the Common Kaili lect Ija (p. 311), not entered as a lect.

name: Kulawi
subgroup_path: Austronesian > Malayo-Polynesian > Celebic > Kaili–Wolio > Northern Kaili–Wolio > Greater Kaili
notes: Glottocode of Moma, the Kulawi language proper; Glottolog's node 'Kulawi' also takes in Lindu.

name: Lindu
subgroup_path: Austronesian > Malayo-Polynesian > Celebic > Kaili–Wolio > Northern Kaili–Wolio > Greater Kaili
notes: Not in Table 18; only the changes stated in the prose of section 4.2.1 (pp. 311-312) are entered.

name: Sedoa
subgroup_path: Austronesian > Malayo-Polynesian > Celebic > Kaili–Wolio > Northern Kaili–Wolio > Greater Kaili
notes: Not in Table 18; only the one change stated in the prose (p. 311) is entered. No Sedoa forms are cited.

name: Topoiyo
notes: Not in Table 18; only the two statements in the prose (p. 311) are entered.

name: Uma
notes: The only Kaili–Wolio language that keeps the PKW final glottal stop (p. 314). Influenced by Badaic (p. 320); daliʔ 'fly' is a Badaic loan and ui 'rattan' a Rampi loan (pp. 326, 340).

name: Pamona
notes: Represents Northern Kaili–Wolio in Tables 3-4. Some cited forms have d for PNKW r (donge 'hear', daa 'blood', -dopo 'fathom'); the source states no rule.

name: Padoe
notes: Cited only in Tables 1-2 (pp. 300-301) as a witness for PCEL final y. The source does not say which Celebic microgroup Padoe belongs to.

name: Saluan
subgroup_path: Austronesian > Malayo-Polynesian > Celebic > Eastern Celebic > Saluan–Banggai
notes: Cited in Tables 1-2 (pp. 300-301) as a witness for PCEL final y and R; Saluan–Banggai membership from fn. 5 and p. 299.

name: Proto-Sumatran
region: Sumatra and the Barrier Islands off its west coast
orthography_note: The source's symbols: ɡ (IPA g), ə for the schwa (PMP e), y for the palatal glide.
notes: Reconstructed by the source from seven pre- and proto-languages (Pre-Gayo, Proto-Batak, Proto-Northern BI, Proto-Central BI, Pre-Mentawai, Pre-Enggano, Pre-Nasal) as a branch of PMP defined by five mergers and one shift (Table 31, p. 133): *j, *g > *ɡ; *z, *d > *d; *R, *r > *r; *ñ, *n > *n; *h > Ø; *q > *h. Inventory from Table 12 (p. 125). Besides the inventory, homorganic nasal-stop sequences (*mb, *nd, *ŋɡ, *mp, *nt, *ŋk) and *rC sequences are reconstructed word-medially, and the vowel sequences *au and *ua; *uə and *əu are only marginally attested (pp. 130, 132). *y is not word-initial; *ə is not found in open word-final syllables (p. 132). PMP *c is not considered: no inherited reflex is attested by several Sumatran languages (pp. 137-138). The Glottolog node Sumatran (suma1277) follows this paper and has the same seven branches.

name: Pre-Gayo
notes: Reconstruction before the split of the Gayo varieties (Bukit, Cik, Dëret, Lues, Serbejadi), from Hazeu (1907), Eades (2005) and Shorto (1976) (section 2.1, pp. 117-118). Inventory from Table 1 (p. 117); also the nasal-stop sequences *mp, *nt, *ŋk. *b, *d, *ɡ are not reconstructed although Hazeu's dictionary has many examples, likely borrowed (pp. 117, 137); /dʒ/ occurs in Malay loans with PMP *z (pp. 133, 137). The correspondence tables write Pre-G *e (Table 26) and *o (Table 29), which are not in Table 1 (ɛ, ə, ɔ); they are entered as printed. Irregular forms shared with Proto-Batak (not entered as rows): *aɡi > *aŋɡi (Pre-G *əŋɡi), and an added final *h in *waluh 'eight' and *siwah 'nine' (p. 141). No glottocode is given here because the attested lect Gayo (gayo1244) is entered separately.

name: Gayo
notes: The source states two correspondence sets among the Gayo varieties (pp. 117-118): the diphthongs of the Lues variety against the mid vowels of Bukit and Dëret, and the 'funny' (post-ploded) nasals, kept apart from plain voiced stops mainly by older speakers (Eades 2005). They are entered here with the variety or generation in the environment; the remaining Pre-Gayo phonemes are entered as unchanged.
inherit_note: Unchanged: the source names only two correspondence sets among the Gayo varieties, the diphthongs and the funny nasals (pp. 117-118).

name: Proto-Batak
notes: Simplified overview following primarily Adelaar (1981) (section 2.2, pp. 118-119). Inventory from Table 2 (p. 118); also *mb, *nd, *ŋɡ, *mp, *nt, *ŋk and *rC sequences between vowels. *c and *j are not word-final, *y is not word-initial. *j is [dʒ] (fn. 4). The source gives no PSUM origin for PB *c and *j: claimed reflexes of PMP *c have no cognates in the other Sumatran languages (pp. 137-138), and /dʒ/ occurs in Malay loans with PMP *z (pp. 133, 137). Glottolog's Batakic (toba1265) also has Alas-Kluet, which the source does not name (it speaks of 'at least seven' Batak languages and lists six).

name: Proto-Northern Batak
notes: Node of Figure 3 (p. 145) and Appendix G (p. 170), ancestor of Dairi and Karo (Adelaar's Northern Batak, p. 118). The source gives no inventory; it is generated from the changes of Appendix G plus the unchanged PB phonemes. Glottolog's Northern Batak (nort2831) also has Alas-Kluet, which the source does not name.
inherit_note: Unchanged: not among the nontrivial sets of Table 3 (p. 119), and no change is stated in Appendix G (p. 170).

name: Proto-CSBatak
notes: Node of Figure 3 (p. 145, 'CSBatak') and Appendix G (p. 170, 'PCSB'), ancestor of Simalungun and of PSB (Toba, Angkola, Mandailing); the abbreviation is not expanded in the source. It has the membership of Adelaar's Southern Batak (p. 118) and of Glottolog's Southern Batak (sout3166). The source gives no inventory; it is generated from the changes of Appendix G plus the unchanged PB phonemes.
inherit_note: Unchanged: not among the nontrivial sets of Table 3 (p. 119), and no change is stated in Appendix G (p. 170).

name: Proto-Southern Batak
notes: Node of Figure 3 (p. 145, 'SBatak') and Appendix G (p. 170, 'PSB'), ancestor of Toba, Angkola and Mandailing only; in the text (p. 118) 'Southern Batak (SB)' is Adelaar's group, which includes Simalungun. Same membership as Glottolog's Tobaic (sout2849). Figure 3 has a further node AM-Batak for Angkola and Mandailing, for which no changes are stated. The source gives no inventory; it is generated.
inherit_note: Unchanged: not among the nontrivial sets of Table 3 (p. 119), and no change is stated in Appendix G (p. 170).

name: Dairi
notes: Reflexes from Table 3 (p. 119) and Appendix G (p. 170); data from Manik (2002). PB phonemes outside the nontrivial sets of Table 3 are entered as unchanged.
inherit_note: Unchanged: not among the nontrivial sets of Table 3 (p. 119), and no change is stated in Appendix G (p. 170).

name: Karo
notes: Reflexes from Table 3 (p. 119) and Appendix G (p. 170); data from Neumann (1951). PB phonemes outside the nontrivial sets of Table 3 are entered as unchanged.
inherit_note: Unchanged: not among the nontrivial sets of Table 3 (p. 119), and no change is stated in Appendix G (p. 170).

name: Simalungun
notes: Reflexes from Table 3 (p. 119) and Appendix G (p. 170); data from Syarfina et al. (2015). PB phonemes outside the nontrivial sets of Table 3 are entered as unchanged. Simalungun, Toba and Angkola geminates correspond to nasal-stop sequences elsewhere; they are written as nasal-stop sequences (fn. 5, p. 118; p. 147).
inherit_note: Unchanged: not among the nontrivial sets of Table 3 (p. 119), and no change is stated in Appendix G (p. 170).

name: Toba
notes: Reflexes from Table 3 (p. 119) and Appendix G (p. 170); data from Warneck (1977). PB phonemes outside the nontrivial sets of Table 3 are entered as unchanged. Simalungun, Toba and Angkola geminates correspond to nasal-stop sequences elsewhere; they are written as nasal-stop sequences (fn. 5, p. 118; p. 147).
inherit_note: Unchanged: not among the nontrivial sets of Table 3 (p. 119), and no change is stated in Appendix G (p. 170).

name: Angkola
subgroup_path: Austronesian > Malayo-Polynesian > Sumatran > Batak > CSBatak > Southern Batak > AM-Batak
notes: Reflexes from Table 3 (p. 119); Appendix G (p. 170) states no change between PSB and Angkola. Data from Eggink (1936). AM-Batak (Figure 3) is not entered as a lect: no changes are stated for it. Simalungun, Toba and Angkola geminates correspond to nasal-stop sequences elsewhere; they are written as nasal-stop sequences (fn. 5, p. 118; p. 147).
inherit_note: Unchanged: Table 3 (p. 119) has the PSB values for Angkola, and Appendix G (p. 170) states no change.

name: Mandailing
subgroup_path: Austronesian > Malayo-Polynesian > Sumatran > Batak > CSBatak > Southern Batak > AM-Batak
notes: Reflexes from Table 3 (p. 119) and Appendix G (p. 170). Mandailing forms are not cited in the source because they are nearly the same as Angkola; the clearest differences are the loss of /h/ and the retention of nasal-stop sequences, not realised as geminates (fn. 9, p. 147). AM-Batak (Figure 3) is not entered as a lect.
inherit_note: Unchanged: not among the nontrivial sets of Table 3 (p. 119), and no change is stated in Appendix G (p. 170). Mandailing forms are not cited in the source (p. 147).

name: Proto-Northern Barrier Islands
region: Pulau Simeulue and Pulau Banyak, Aceh
notes: Ancestor of Haloban, Leukon and Simeulue (section 2.3, pp. 120-121). Inventory from Table 4 (p. 120), except that the high diphthong printed *uy there is entered as *oy, the form of Tables 5 and 30 and Appendices F and G. Also the sequences *mb, *nd, *mp, *nt, *ŋk between vowels. *b and *d are not word-final; *r, *w, *y, *ʔ are not word-initial; *p occurs only word-finally and between vowels after *ə. The status of final *s is unclear (fn. 26, p. 151). Finer vowel developments in the NBI languages are left aside by the source (p. 150). /dʒ/ occurs in Malay loans with PMP *z (pp. 133, 137). No glottocode: Glottolog has Haloban and Leukon as dialects of the language Simeulue (sime1241), not as a family.

name: Haloban
notes: Reflexes from Table 5 (p. 121) and Appendix G (p. 170); data from Tim Kamus Balai Bahasa Banda Aceh (2013). Treated by the source as one of three NBI languages; a dialect of Simeulue in Glottolog. PNBI phonemes outside the nontrivial sets of Table 5 are entered as unchanged.
inherit_note: Unchanged: not among the nontrivial sets of Table 5 (p. 121).

name: Leukon
notes: Reflexes from Table 5 (p. 121) and Appendix G (p. 170); data from Candrasari & Khalsiah (2018) and Kähler (1961). Treated by the source as one of three NBI languages; a dialect of Simeulue in Glottolog. PNBI phonemes outside the nontrivial sets of Table 5 are entered as unchanged.
inherit_note: Unchanged: not among the nontrivial sets of Table 5 (p. 121).

name: Simeulue
notes: Reflexes from Table 5 (p. 121) and Appendix G (p. 170); data from Kähler (1961). PNBI phonemes outside the nontrivial sets of Table 5 are entered as unchanged.
inherit_note: Unchanged: not among the nontrivial sets of Table 5 (p. 121).

name: Proto-Central Barrier Islands
notes: Ancestor of Sigulai and Nias (section 2.4, pp. 121-122). Inventory from Table 6 (p. 121). No word-final consonants and no word-final diphthongs; the medial sequences *mb and *nd (not *ŋɡ) are reconstructed. *ʔ, *x, *r, *y are not word-initial. An adjacent PSUM *r, itself lost, changed the vowels: *a, *ə, *u > *o and *i > *e, in the vowel next to initial or final *r, in the leftmost of two identical vowels, or in the vowel lowest on the hierarchy i > u > a > ə of two unlike vowels; *ara > *o (p. 130). Excrescent nasals in single words (fn. 33-35, pp. 152-153) are not entered. Same membership as Glottolog's Nias-Sikule (nias1241).

name: Sigulai
notes: Reflexes from Table 7 (p. 122) and Appendix G (p. 170); data from Kähler (1959). PCBI phonemes outside the nontrivial sets of Table 7 are entered as unchanged.
inherit_note: Unchanged: not among the nontrivial sets of Table 7 (p. 122).

name: Nias
notes: Reflexes from Table 7 (p. 122) and Appendix G (p. 170); data from Sundermann (1905). PCBI phonemes outside the nontrivial sets of Table 7 are entered as unchanged.
inherit_note: Unchanged: not among the nontrivial sets of Table 7 (p. 122).

name: Pre-Mentawai
notes: Reconstruction before the split of the Mentawai varieties, from Pampus (1989, 1994), Lenggang (1992) and Morris (1900) (section 2.5, pp. 122-123). Inventory from Table 8 (p. 122); nasal-stop sequences are also reconstructed. Voiced stops are not word-final, *j is only medial, *k and *s are not word-final. The correspondence tables also give Pre-M *w (from final *ɡ and *k, forming a diphthong with a preceding *a or *ə, p. 126) and *uy (Table 30), which are not in Table 8; they are entered as printed. No glottocode is given here because the attested lect Mentawai (ment1249) is entered separately.

name: Mentawai
notes: A group of diverse varieties. The source states four nontrivial correspondence sets among them without a table (p. 123): final nasals and final voiceless stops (kept apart in some varieties, merged as stops or as nasals in others), geminate stops against nasal-stop sequences (the nasal assimilates fully to the stop in some varieties; not entered as rows, the clusters are not listed), and initial d against r. The merger of *s and *t as t in the Simalegi variety is from p. 143. The remaining Pre-Mentawai phonemes are entered as unchanged.
inherit_note: Unchanged: the source names only four nontrivial correspondence sets among the Mentawai varieties (p. 123).

name: Pre-Enggano
notes: Reconstruction before the split of the Enggano dialects, from the data up to Kähler (1987), largely after Edwards (2015) (section 2.6, pp. 123-124). Inventory from Table 9 (p. 123). No coda consonants and no word-final diphthongs. Nasality is a word-level feature: PSUM coda nasals, and final *l and *r (after *i) through a merger with *n, made the word nasal unless *ə preceded, and were then lost; the nasals themselves became *b, *d and (through *ɡ) *h. A '~' in the source's tables marks a reflex in a nasal word; it is given in the notes here. The source orders the changes in three stages (Table 39, pp. 138-140): 1. *b, *p > *p; *s, *t > *t; loss of *h; changes of *r; *k > *ʔ. 2. *w > *b; *t > *k; suprasegmentalisation of nasality. 3. *ɡ > *h; loss of codas. Edwards (2015) reconstructs *t where the source has *d for the d/r : t set (p. 124). No glottocode is given here because the attested lect Enggano (engg1245) is entered separately.

name: Enggano
notes: Old Enggano: the language up to and including Kähler's (1987) dictionary. The two columns of Table 10 (p. 124), South and West, are the dialects of that period; they are entered with the dialect in the environment. Later changes (Yoder 2014, Edwards 2015: erosion of final vowels, split of /o/ into /o/ and /ɘ/; p. 140) are not entered. The remaining Pre-Enggano phonemes are entered as unchanged.
inherit_note: Unchanged: not among the nontrivial sets of Table 10 (p. 124).

name: Pre-Nasal
notes: Reconstruction for Nasal, which has no known dialect differences; based on the authors' documentation (McDonnell 2017a, b, 2019) and earlier wordlists (section 2.7, pp. 124-125). Inventory from Table 11 (p. 125). *b, *d, *ɡ are not word-final and *y is not word-initial; *o (from *a) and *ʔ (contrasting with *k) are only word-final. The voiced obstruents are kept next to *ə and in nasal-stop sequences; elsewhere *b > *w, *d > *χ, *ɡ > *h, and word-finally they are devoiced. Most other b, d, ɡ of modern Nasal are borrowed, and /r/ for PMP *j is attributed to Lampungic loans (pp. 125, 137); /dʒ/ occurs in Malay loans with PMP *z (pp. 133, 137). Nasal gives no clear evidence for or against the merger of *ñ and *n (pp. 134-135). No separate lect is entered for modern Nasal: the source states no change after Pre-N.

name: Proto-Bima-Lembata
notes: Node of the classification tree in Grimes & Edwards (2026: 164) (§3.4). As printed: *b > **β, **b. The source finds nothing in the historical phonology that links the Wallacean subgroups below PMP (p. 25). No inventory is given; it is generated from the reflexes. Glottocode bima1248 (Bima-Lembata): the Glottolog clade with the same member languages.

name: Proto-East Sumbawa
notes: Node of the classification tree in Grimes & Edwards (2026: 164) (§3.4). As printed: *-ay > e, *-aw > o, *R > ∅ (all also in Komodo). No inventory is given; it is generated from the reflexes. Glottocode east2913 (East Sumbawa): the Glottolog clade with the same member languages.

name: Sanggar
notes: Classification tree, p. 164. Appendix A (p. 730): ISO ---, glottocode sang1334.

name: Bima
notes: Classification tree, p. 164. As printed: *p > f, p; *t > d, t; *k > h, k; *q > ∅; **b > ɓ, b, mb, w; *d/*z > r, ɗ; *j/*l > r, l; *s > s, ʧ; *R > ∅, r; *w > w, ∅; *y > ʤ; *ə > i, e, a, o, u; *-ay > e; *-aw > o; *-iw > u; *-uy > i. name: Proto-North-Central Vanuatu

The intermediate stages Proto-Eastern Oceanic and Proto-Southern Oceanic, which the source also cites, are not entered. Clark writes PNCV *R where an etymon keeps *R in some NCV languages and loses it in others, and *r where all NCV languages keep it; all non-zero reflexes of *R in NCV are identical with those of *r (p. 149). Root-final *R is lost with all word-final consonants, a late change in the history of the linkage (p. 151). François finds that *R-loss spread word by word from the south: for each etymon the languages keeping *R lie north of the isogloss and those losing it south of it (pp. 155-156, 166-168, 15 isoglosses). Glottocode nort3195 (North and Central Vanuatu). No inventory is given; it is generated from the reflexes.

name: Proto-Punan
notes: Punan Tubu, Punan Bah, Punan Aput, Beketan, Ukit and others (Smith 2017a: 111-127; Figure 27, p. 112). 'Proto-Punan had not undergone any major changes'; the subgroup rests on lexical innovations, above all the metathesis *təlaʔus > *təlasuʔ 'barking deer' (p. 114). Smith treats Punan as one language with dialects (p. 120). His internal split into Punan Tubu-Bah and the rest (Figures 28-29, pp. 122-124) has conflicting evidence (p. 122), so no lower nodes are entered; the changes are entered on each lect. Table 31 has '?' for PMP *r. Glottolog's Punan (puna1280) follows Smith's grouping.
